identity.title: Presenting (academic skills pathway)
identity.agentDefinition: Presenting is one of thirteen academic skills pathways: creating and delivering presentations as assessment and as a transferable skill, from how a presentation is put together (five steps, structure), through delivering it well across formats (visual aids and accessibility, nerves, individual, poster, group, professional, interview-based and technology-based presentations), to presenting with authority and working in groups (academic voice, defending an argument under questioning, professional formats, leadership and conflict resolution). Reach for it to place, sequence or assess a capability in oral and visual communication or group work, or to translate one into its workplace form. It is not about writing (Academic Writing), nor about reflection as a practice, which the group work's reflective element draws on (Reflective Practice).
identity.summary: The academic skills pathways model (2026) sets Presenting as one of thirteen pathways, drawn from one chapter of a study skills guide on creating presentations and working in groups. It climbs in three tiers: what a presentation is and how one is put together (reading the brief, the five steps, a hook, one point per slide, a conclusion that returns to the objectives); delivering it well across formats (the six types of presentation, "less is more" and accessible visual aids, managing nerves and avoiding the classic errors); and presenting with authority and collaborating (academic voice, asserting and defending an argument under questioning, the pitch, the conference poster and the viva-style interview in depth, and group work: personality types, leadership and conflict resolution, and the reflective element tutors assess). The guide frames both presentations and group work as transferable skills and parts of graduate identity, often tested at interview. The model flags that group work could become a pathway of its own and that the pathway is less writing-centric than most, to be pressure-tested before it is built. Its open questions are an Introductory tier with no capability, the place of group work and which theory to make key (Part E).

tierProgression.masteryNote: Across the tiers the weight moves along Anderson and Krathwohl's continuum: Introductory is mostly declarative and procedural, the recipe for a presentation, with a first check of one's own performance in practice; Intermediate is procedural, design and delivery across formats, with the self-system entering as the learner manages their own nerves; Advanced is metacognitive, the learner presenting in professional forms, working in a team and defending an argument as someone with standing in their field. In Marzano and Kendall's terms the self-system, beliefs about oneself and one's emotional response, is unusually present in this pathway from the start. Mastery is presenting and collaborating as a professional, the map's Advanced goal, which is the core's A11 ladder from compliance to flow.

theorySpine.overview:
- Three tiers, Introductory, Intermediate and Advanced, each with a focus, content and a goal (D:PTM, Pathway 7).
- The tiers were remapped by the model's author on 3 September 2026: the mechanics of building a presentation moved to Introductory and the types of presentation to Intermediate; Advanced returns to three formats from the Intermediate list in more depth (D:PTM, Pathway 7, note).
- Group work folds in at Advanced and may spin out into its own pathway later; the pathway is less writing-centric and is to be pressure-tested before it is built (D:PTM, Pathway 7, flags).
- Tiers are anchored to experience of the practice, not to year of study (D:TSPEC, section 2).
theorySpine.corePrinciples:
- Presentations test many of the literacies of written work, argument, critique of the discourse and clear communication, but orally, in front of an audience, with visual aids and constraints such as a time limit and questions (D:EAU, p. 201).
- A presentation develops the student's academic voice: asserting and defending an argument under questioning gives ownership of one's understanding and disciplinary knowledge (D:EAU, p. 201).
- Presenting and working in groups are transferable skills valued by employers and often tested at interview; a presentation in selection is a statement of graduate identity (D:EAU, pp. 200, 202).
- Tutors use different types of presentation, each with its own expectations: individual, poster, group, professional or practice-based, interview-based and technology-based (D:EAU, pp. 203-204).
- A presentation is created in five steps: read the instructions, research the topic, plan, design visual aids, then put it together and practise (D:EAU, pp. 206-208).
- Visual aids complement the spoken content and should not distract; "less is more", and design should consider accessibility for visually impaired and dyslexic audiences (D:EAU, pp. 208-209).
- A presentation has an introduction with a hook and signposted objectives, a main body arranged logically with one point per slide, and a conclusion that returns to the objectives (D:EAU, pp. 209-210).
- Nerves are normal; project confidence, engage the audience, know the room and its technology, keep to time and prepare for questions (D:EAU, pp. 206, 210-212).
- In group work tutors value the process over the product, and assessment often includes a reflective element on one's contribution (D:EAU, pp. 212-213).
- Awareness of personality types, after the five-factor model, helps a group member resolve conflict and work with others (D:EAU, pp. 216-217, after McCrae and Costa, 1999). [The pathway does not teach it: group work is taught through process (D-ing-0054).]
theorySpine.selection: Choose this pathway when the aim is oral and visual communication of academic work, or working with others on an assessed task. For writing, choose `path:academic-writing`; for reflecting on a group task, `path:reflective-practice`; for professional practice settings, `path:work-based-experiential-learning`; for research posters' content, `path:researching-research-methods`. It suits badly a learner whose need is a written genre.

analysis: **The guide's vocabulary against the benchmarks':** the guide says the five steps, hook, main body, conclusion, less is more, accessibility, nerves, poster, pitch, interview-based, leadership, conflict; the benchmarks say oral presentations, audio-visual aids, audience, debates, critiques, posters, collaboration and group work. Both belong in the practice searcher's vocabulary for this pathway.
**Skill against theme:** one of the nine extracts is skill; adp-0212 found nothing for the hook and nerves card (d3).

**Book coverage:** Chapter 11 carries all nine cards, and the five steps, the types of presentation, visual aids, structure, Nasser's nerves and Ross's group are all there; the guide does not develop academic voice as such (e3 draws on its "articulate an argument").

**Other authors:** META holds Gibbs (1994) and Healey (2024) for group work; the strand leads for the rest (Aristotle, Mayer, Tufte, McCroskey, Ivanič) are wanted (W-0076, W-0066, W-0078, W-0067, W-0064).

Nothing names managing one's own anxiety (d3) or academic voice (e3); they sit in Marzano and Kendall's self-system, which the frameworks do not describe.

gaps.coreOpenQuestions:
1. **P2 triggers:** 4 and 5: the five-factor model, Mayer, the level descriptors and Vitae were read by summary only; McCroskey, Tuckman and Belbin are recall only (W-0065 to W-0068, W-0031 to W-0034). The crosswalk is editorial. [14:50: the strand research adds Garner and Alley, Tuckman, cooperative learning, social loafing, Edmondson and Belbin by summary, and Joughin, McCroskey and Bodie by citation only (W-0070 to W-0076).]
2. **Levels:** `unknown` for every capability (D-ing-0001 (a)).
3. **Capability coverage:** settled (D-ing-0051, Abbott, 14:06). No card sits at Introductory, which holds the building of a presentation (the brief, the five steps, structure). At Advanced, `/04` covers group work only; academic voice, defending an argument under questioning and the three professional formats have no card. Candidates for the model's author, temporary ids: c1 (Introductory) "Build a presentation to a brief through the five steps, with a hook, a main body and a conclusion"; c2 (Advanced) "Present and defend an argument with an academic voice under questioning"; c3 (Advanced) "Present in professional formats: the pitch, the conference poster and the viva-style interview". [Settled: all three, c1 at Introductory, c2 at Intermediate (not Advanced, as ing proposed), c3 at Advanced. ing had recommended (b), c1 and c2 only.]
4. **Key theory:** settled in part (D-ing-0052, Abbott, 14:50): by strand. The guide cites no theory of presenting; for group work it cites the five-factor model. Candidates: Mayer's multimedia learning (visual aids), McCroskey's communication apprehension (nerves), Tuckman and Belbin (group work), Ivanič (academic voice). None is ingested. [D-ing-0052 (a), with more research: five strands and their theorists in A9. Proposed leads, not ruled: Aristotle (building and structure), Mayer (visual aids), McCroskey (delivery and nerves), Ivanič (academic voice), Tuckman (group work). All read by summary, abstract or citation only (W-0064 to W-0076).] [15:19, Abbott: Gibbs also writes on group work; added: Gibbs (1994) and his review of group work assessment, with his reflective cycle (META run) for the group reflection (W-0077).] [08:42, settled (D-ing-0053, Abbott): the leads as proposed, except group work, led by Gibbs (1994) and Healey (2024) with Tuckman beside; visual aids gain a visual design voice beside Mayer: Tufte (2003), with Williams (2015) and Kosslyn (2007) (W-0078 to W-0080).]
5. **Group work:** the model flags that it may spin out into its own pathway; here it is one Advanced card.
6. **Conflict, the five-factor model:** the guide maps each factor to a personality type and calls neuroticism "realists" (p. 217); the model treats the factors as continuous traits and defines neuroticism by unpleasant emotion and vulnerability. Recorded as a conflict; the lessons need a ruling before they teach OCEAN. [08:42, settled (D-ing-0054, Abbott): OCEAN is left out of the teaching; group work is taught through process (roles, stages, agreed ways of working). The model's Advanced tier text (A3) still names personality types (OCEAN): that is the model author's text, for its next revision.]
7. **Pressure-test:** the model asks for the pathway to be pressure-tested before it is built, being less writing-centric.
8. **Templates:** proposed: a presentation plan, a slide design checklist with accessibility and a group work reflection.
9. **Progression by level (A11):** drafted with the document (J-ing-0001; META D-0205; D-ing-0035, D-ing-0036, D-ing-0038, D-ing-0039). Every level was read by summary only.
10. **Source map:** what *Excelling at University* teaches for each capability is in its source map, not here.
11. **Vocabulary (D-ing-0050):** built in from the start: the glossary term for this pathway in B2a, candidates from the model's tier text and the candidate theories in B2b, A10's direct terms as the term list v1.0 patterns. The search patterns themselves are kept with each consuming project.
